parakeet: People often try to smooth over the tension between faith and science with the simple phrase, they're both valid, they just exist in different realms. On the surface, that sounds clever enough to be true. It explains why scientific tests never confirm miracles, yet faith still has millions of followers. It allows the believer to say, of course science can't prove God. It's not supposed to. And for a moment, that truth feels tidy, like the perfect compromise. Science handles the material world, faith handles the spiritual world. Whatever that is. Part of what makes this claim appealing is that it buys peace. It gives both sides a way to stop fighting without either side admitting defeat. It reassures the believer that their faith hasn't been made obsolete by discovery or technology, and it reinsures the scientists that they won't be forced into a debate about angels, demons, or prayer. It's like everyone gets to keep their own sandbox, no questions asked. But here's the catch. Neat compromises like this usually hide bigger problems. Because if we actually take this claim seriously, if we grant that faith and science are both valid, but in different realms, then we have to ask what validity even means. Science proves its validity by producing results. Medicine that heals, technology that works, knowledge that predicts. So what about faith? If it is valid in its own realm, then surely it should be able to prove itself by its own standards in its own context. That's where things start to unravel.
